tagline: Wooded roads, a stone bridge and gardens along the Brandywine
intro: The Brandywine Valley Scenic Byway links wooded roads, fields and creek crossings in southeastern Pennsylvania. Kennett Pike has two undivided lanes; the shared stretch with US 1 broadens to four lanes divided by a median. PennDOT designated its corridor along PA 52, PA 162 and Old Creek Road in 2005. The Federal Highway Administration identifies commerce, agriculture, artistic creativity and political thought as defining strands of the valley, and notes structures associated with the Underground Railroad along the byway.

The road numbers came long after some of the routes they mark. Between Marshallton and West Chester, part of PA 162 follows the Great Minquas Path and became part of Strasburg Road in the 1770s. PA 52 changed again in 2011, when a new alignment opened north of US 1 to improve traffic flow; part of the former road became an entrance road for Longwood Gardens.

Coming north from Delaware, Kennett Pike passes through wooded residential country before joining US 1 at Hamorton. PA 52 leaves US 1 near Longwood Gardens, winds toward Lenape and crosses the Brandywine on Lenape Bridge. It then follows Creek Road briefly before continuing along Lenape Road toward West Chester. The PA 162 branch approaches the borough from the west along Strasburg Road.

moments.title: Longwood Gardens
moments.text: Longwood began with trees threatened by timber cutting. Samuel and Joshua Peirce began planting an arboretum on their inherited farm in 1798. When a lumber operator prepared to fell the trees in 1906, Pierre S. du Pont bought the property primarily to preserve them. He added the Flower Garden Walk in 1907 and opened the garden to the public in 1921. Peirce’s Park remains part of the gardens, with the Sylvan Fountain that du Pont added in 1925–27. The enlarged brick farmhouse built by Joshua Peirce in 1730 also survives.

moments.title: Lenape
moments.text: Lenape Bridge carries PA 52 across the Brandywine Creek and a parking lot beyond it. Built in 1911–1912 from random rubble stone, the bridge has seven arches, each spanning 44 feet. The whole structure measures 308 feet. On the western side of the creek, the community of Lenape centers on PA 52 and Pocopson Road. An East Penn Railroad line crosses PA 52 at grade just before the road reaches the creek. Across the bridge, PA 52 turns onto Creek Road, the former alignment of PA 100, before continuing along Lenape Road.
moments.notice: Seven stone arches carry the crossing, each spanning 44 feet.

moments.title: Strasburg Road
moments.text: Strasburg Road carries a route older than Pennsylvania’s highway numbers. Between Marshallton and West Chester, PA 162 follows the seventeenth-century Great Minquas Path. John Sellers and others surveyed this section in 1772 and 1773 under Governor Richard Penn as part of the road linking Strasburg and Philadelphia. Construction was completed under the government of independent Pennsylvania. When PA 162 received its number in 1928, the section between Embreeville and West Chester was already paved. The approach to West Chester now crosses the East Branch Brandywine Creek on Cope’s Bridge, then passes increasing residential development.
